enrichment.short_title: Assault on police officer during lawful search and handcuffing
key_facts: Mr Collman was convicted by magistrates of assaulting PC Logan in the execution of his duty after resisting a lawful empty-pockets and pat-down search following arrest.
The justices found the officers had reasonable grounds under PACE section 32(1) and that force used in searching and handcuffing was reasonable.
On appeal by case stated, Collman challenged the finding of Cunningham recklessness and the lawfulness of retaining his possessions for the duration of the search.
Kay J held the retention method was a reasonable way to conduct the search where officers intended to return all items at its conclusion.
The case stated disclosed ample evidence from which magistrates could infer recklessness; the appeal was dismissed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' conviction to the Administrative Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; both questions answered in the negative.
enrichment.ratio: Where a lawful search under PACE section 32(1) is in progress, officers may lawfully retain items taken from pockets until the search concludes if that is a reasonable methodology and they intend to return lawful possessions; sufficiency of evidence for Cunningham recklessness is a matter for the magistrates where bodily movements and circumstances support an inference of foresight.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates erred in finding recklessness on the evidence
Whether police acted lawfully in retaining the appellant's possessions during the search rather than returning items one by one
Whether officers were acting in the lawful execution of their duty
Application of Cunningham recklessness to common assault and battery

enrichment.short_title: CFA disclosure and enforceability on costs assessment
key_facts: The Court of Appeal heard six consolidated appeals on conditional fee agreements, disclosure on costs assessment, and compliance with the CFA Regulations 2000.
The court held that Bailey v IBC Vehicles should not be extended to exempt CFAs from normal disclosure where a success fee materially increases the paying party's liability.
A CFA is unenforceable only if departures from section 58 conditions had a materially adverse effect on client protection or the administration of justice.
Claimants' appeals succeeded in Hollins v Russell and Tichband v Hurdman; defendants' disclosure appeals succeeded in Worth v McKenna and Pratt v Bull.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated appeals to the Court of Appeal on detailed assessment of costs and CFA enforceability.
enrichment.outcome: Mixed result across six appeals; court set out procedural and substantive principles for CFA disclosure and assessment.
enrichment.ratio: CFAs should normally be disclosed for costs proceedings where a success fee is claimed; enforceability depends on whether any non-compliance with section 58 or the Regulations materially adversely affected client protection or the administration of justice, not on technical breaches alone.
legal_issues: Whether receiving parties must disclose CFAs on detailed assessment
Whether non-compliance with CFA Regulations renders agreements unenforceable
Application of the indemnity principle to success fees
Whether Bailey v IBC Vehicles applies to CFAs
Materiality of regulatory breaches on costs recovery

enrichment.short_title: HSE liability for Ladbroke Grove rail crash

statutes_considered.title: Railway and Other Transport Systems (Approval of Works, Plant and Equipment) Regulations 1994
Health and Safety at Work Act 1974

key_facts: Thirty-one people died when a Thames Trains service passed signal SN109 at danger and collided head-on at Ladbroke Grove in October 1999.
Thames Trains sought contribution from the HSE, alleging breach of statutory duty and common law negligence in failing to ensure safe signalling infrastructure.
Morland J refused to strike out the claim; the HSE appealed under CPR rule 3.4(2).
The Court of Appeal held Regulation 4 did not give passengers a private law cause of action for breach of statutory duty.
The court declined to strike out the common law negligence claim, finding arguable duties by assumption of responsibility and distinguishing Stovin v Wise on the pleaded facts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal to strike out contribution claim as disclosing no reasonable grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; common law negligence claim to proceed to trial; no private right under Regulation 4.
enrichment.ratio: Regulatory approval provisions protecting the public at large do not ordinarily confer a private damages action; where a statutory regulator's alleged failures are pleaded with sufficient particularity and may involve assumed responsibility or active conduct rather than mere omission, strike-out is inappropriate in developing areas of public authority liability.
legal_issues: Whether Regulation 4 creates a private law cause of action
Whether the HSE owed a common law duty of care to rail passengers
Application of Stovin v Wise to non-exercise of statutory powers
Whether assumption of responsibility can found liability for the HSE
Appropriateness of strike-out in uncertain developing law

enrichment.short_title: Bank fraud freezing order and forum challenge

statutes_considered.title: Foreign Exchange (Monitoring and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1995

key_facts: Claimants traced $190m misapplied from Banco Noroeste through international transfers and sought recovery from substantive and conspiracy defendants.
Mr Vaswani was joined as the forty-second defendant and a worldwide freezing order for US$6.5m was granted ex parte by Lightman J.
Vaswani applied to set aside the freezing order for material non-disclosure and to stay proceedings on forum non conveniens grounds.
The Vice-Chancellor found minor non-disclosures but no injustice warranting discharge; the Sarina account had been frozen in Switzerland.
England was held the appropriate forum given multi-party claims, central role of Naresh Asnani, and unsuitability of Lagos court procedure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Inter partes application to set aside worldwide freezing order and stay English proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; freezing undertakings and security upheld; no stay to Nigeria.
enrichment.ratio: Minor non-disclosures on ex parte freezing applications do not require discharge where the claim has merit and the defendant voluntarily continued undertakings; in multi-jurisdictional fraud litigation the court may retain all related claims in England where splitting proceedings would risk inconsistent findings and the defendant has not shown Nigeria is clearly and distinctly more appropriate.
legal_issues: Material non-disclosure on ex parte freezing order application
Whether England is the appropriate forum for Vaswani's good-faith purchaser defence
Whether forum analysis is limited to bilateral issues or considers the action as a whole
Risk of dissipation and proportionality of freezing relief

enrichment.short_title: Harrods libel service and forum over WSJ article
key_facts: Harrods issued an April Fool's Day press release about floating the store; The Wall Street Journal published an article comparing Harrods to Enron.
Harrods sued Dow Jones in England for limited UK publication; Dow Jones challenged service and sought a stay for forum non conveniens.
Service at 10 Fleet Place through Dow Jones International Ltd was held ineffective because Dow Jones & Company Inc had not established a place of business in Great Britain.
Eady J granted permission to serve out of the jurisdiction and refused a stay, finding England the appropriate forum for an English company's reputation.
The primary US circulation and First Amendment considerations did not outweigh the separate English cause of action.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications on validity of service, permission to serve out, and forum non conveniens in defamation proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Service at Fleet Place invalid; permission to serve out granted; stay refused.
enrichment.ratio: Default service under section 695 requires an overseas company to have established a place of business in Great Britain, distinct from merely carrying on business through a separate English subsidiary; an English company may pursue a separate English publication defamation claim here despite wider foreign circulation, and damage is presumed without de minimis exclusion.
legal_issues: Whether Dow Jones established a place of business at Fleet Place for section 695 service
Distinction between carrying on business and establishing a place of business
Whether England is forum non conveniens where primary publication was in the United States
Application of Adams v Cape Industries criteria
Separate publication doctrine in English defamation law

enrichment.short_title: Youth court wrongly declined robbery jurisdiction
key_facts: A 14-year-old, C, was charged with attempted robbery of a mobile phone with a co-defendant; no weapon was used though one was threatened.
The Balham Youth Court declined jurisdiction, apparently because no custodial sentence was available there and Crown Court powers were needed.
C had one caution and was not a persistent offender, so a detention and training order under section 100 was unavailable.
Scott Baker LJ held the youth court applied the wrong test and should have retained jurisdiction.
The committal was quashed and the case remitted to the youth court.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of youth court decision declining jurisdiction and committing for Crown Court trial.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review granted; committal quashed; case remitted to youth court.
enrichment.ratio: A youth court should not decline jurisdiction merely because a detention and training order is unavailable for an under-15 non-persistent offender; section 91 long custodial powers are for exceptional cases and declining jurisdiction to preserve theoretical Crown Court sentencing options is ordinarily wrong where no realistic section 91 sentence of two years or more is in prospect.
legal_issues: When a youth court may decline jurisdiction under section 24(1)(a)
Relationship between section 91 and section 100 for offenders under 15
Whether unavailability of a detention and training order justifies committal to Crown Court
Appropriate sentencing for attempted mobile phone robbery by young offenders

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Orange subcontracted mechanical services to ABB on a hospital project; ABB terminated the subcontract in July 2002 and denied Orange site access.
Orange submitted a final account in December 2002 claiming about £204,000 net and referred the dispute to adjudication in January 2003.
ABB argued no dispute had crystallised because it had not finished evaluating the final account and contractual payment machinery had not run its course.
The adjudicator found repudiatory breach and awarded Orange about £90,000 including interest.
Judge Thornton granted summary judgment enforcing both adjudication decisions, holding a dispute existed by 6 January 2003 under the Halki test.
enrichment.procedural_posture: CPR Part 24 summary judgment application to enforce adjudicator's decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment granted; adjudicator had jurisdiction; ABB ordered to pay adjudicator's award.
enrichment.ratio: A dispute for adjudication purposes arises when a claimed sum is not admitted or paid; after repudiatory termination the contractual final-account timetable does not prevent crystallisation, and a reasonable period after submission of a comprehensive final account suffices even over the Christmas period.
legal_issues: When a dispute crystallises for statutory adjudication
Whether DOM/1 final account machinery prevents adjudication after repudiatory breach

enrichment.short_title: Planning enforcement of quarry workshop removal
key_facts: Westhorpe Farm had 1952 planning permission for gravel extraction subject to removal of buildings on completion.

Matthews & Brown Engineering used a workshop for non-ancillary engineering; time limits barred enforcement of the change of use but Enforcement Notice No. 4 required removal of structures after quarrying ended.
North West Estates acquired the land knowing of the unappealed notice and sought to resist a section 187B mandatory injunction.
The Court of Appeal held section 285 prevented challenging the validity of the unappealed notice at the injunction stage.
The established engineering use could not override the condition requiring removal once mineral working had ceased.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from mandatory planning injunction under section 187B to enforce unappealed enforcement notice.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; mandatory removal injunction affirmed.
enrichment.ratio: An unappealed enforcement notice protected by section 285 must be obeyed and its validity cannot be re-argued on a section 187B injunction application; a condition requiring removal of buildings after quarrying ends may lawfully affect even established uses carved out as separate planning units, and fraud in obtaining tolerance does not assist the landowner in resisting enforcement.
legal_issues: Effect of section 285 privative provision on unappealed enforcement notices
Whether established use protects a workshop from Condition 4 removal requirement
Mansi-type amendment defence at injunction stage
Exercise of discretion under section 187B
Whether a planning condition can restrict an established use

enrichment.short_title: Greek distributorship terminated under English law
key_facts: ACI terminated a 1993 English-law distributorship agreement with NOS for Greece after serving notice under clause 10.3.1 for failure to remedy breaches within 30 days.
NOS argued a new Greek-law contract arose from conduct in 2000 and that commercial agent regulations required reasonable notice.
Eady J granted summary judgment declarations that the agreement was validly terminated and NOS must perform clause 11 post-termination obligations.
NOS was a distributor purchasing for resale, not a commercial agent under the Regulations.
The implied Greek-law contract argument was held fanciful for Part 24 purposes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 24 summary judgment application for declarations on termination of distributorship agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment granted; declarations made as to valid termination and post-termination obligations.
enrichment.ratio: A contractual termination under an express remediable-breach clause takes effect if breaches are not remedied within 30 days and need not await negotiation; a distributor taking financial risk is not a commercial agent entitled to reasonable notice, and an unpleaded implied superseding contract governed by foreign law has no real prospect of success.
legal_issues: Whether ACI validly terminated under clause 10.3.1
Whether exclusive English jurisdiction clause governs
Whether NOS was a commercial agent entitled to reasonable notice
Whether conduct superseded the 1993 agreement with a Greek-law contract
Enforcement of clause 11 post-termination obligations

enrichment.short_title: Without prejudice privilege and perjury exception
key_facts: Berry Trade and Vitol sued Mr Ghadimi for conspiracy and deceit over misappropriated oil cargoes; he counterclaimed for management fees.
During without prejudice settlement meetings Ghadimi allegedly said his fee agreement was US$2 per metric tonne, inconsistent with his pleaded US$9 rate.
David Steel J allowed the claimants to adduce the statements on the basis of a serious risk of perjury.
The Court of Appeal held the judge applied too low a test and that disputed admissions from lengthy unrecorded negotiations did not show unambiguous impropriety.
Permission to appeal was granted; the order allowing admission of without prejudice statements was set aside.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal and appeal against interlocutory order admitting without prejudice statements in evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; order admitting without prejudice statements set aside.
enrichment.ratio: The without prejudice rule is breached only in the clearest cases of unambiguous impropriety such as threats or fraud, not where pleaded and oral positions are merely inconsistent; disputed oral admissions from hours of unscripted settlement discussions cannot establish a cloak for perjury, and the correct test is not a serious and substantial risk of perjury.
legal_issues: Without prejudice rule and unambiguous impropriety exception
Whether inconsistent settlement statements may be adduced to prove perjury
